title: AB 325 Cartwright Act: violations (Common pricing algorithms)
requirement: It is unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination or conspiracy to restrain trade, or to use or distribute one while coercing another person to adopt its recommended price or commercial term. A common pricing algorithm is any methodology used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set or influence a price or commercial term. Complaints need only plausibly allege a contract, combination or conspiracy.
penalty: Violations of the Cartwright Act are punishable as a crime; the bill states it creates a new crime or infraction.
citation: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729 (added by AB 325, Stats. 2025, ch. 338)
status_basis: Approved by Governor October 06, 2025; the chunk states no effective date. [effective_date 2026-01-01 from D028]

coverage.summary: Applies to any person using or distributing a common pricing algorithm, across all products and services, not only housing.
coverage.exemptions_summary: The term 'person' does not include the end consumer of a product or service.

precedence.text: Nothing in this section shall impair or limit the applicability of antitrust laws.

quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: Businesses are expressly prohibited from using or distributing common pricing algorithms as part of an agreement to restrain trade.

penalty: City Attorney or aggrieved tenant may sue for damages, injunctive relief, restitution of illegal profits (City Attorney) and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation; prevailing party gets reasonable attorney's fees and costs.

status_basis: Document shows the ordinance was passed to print on 2025-11-18 and was on the 2025-12-02 council agenda; adoption and effective dates are not stated.

exempt_if.text: short-term rentals

exempt_if.name: educational_religious_nonprofit_facilities
exempt_if.text: dwelling units in facilities operated solely for educational, religious, or nonprofit purposes

coverage.summary: Would have applied to most residential rental units statewide.
coverage.exemptions_summary: Exempts owner-occupied buildings of four or fewer units, units under 10 years old, certain publicly regulated units, short-term rentals, and facilities operated solely for educational, religious or nonprofit purposes.

quoted_span: Under the proposed law, annual rent increases would have been limited to the lesser of the annual increase in the Consumer Price Index or 5%.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: The proposal limits annual rent increases for residences, but it carved out exemptions for several types of units, including ones “operated solely for … religious … purposes."

title: Massachusetts Fair Housing Act (G.L. c. 151B, § 4(10)) – public assistance and housing subsidy discrimination
requirement: It is unlawful for anyone furnishing rental accommodations to discriminate against an individual because they receive public assistance or a housing subsidy, including rental assistance, or because of any requirement of such a program.

coverage.summary: Applies to any person furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations to recipients of public assistance or housing subsidies.

quoted_span: For any person furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations to discriminate against any individual who is a recipient of federal, state, or local public assistance, including medical assistance, or who is a tenant receiving federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rental supplements, because the individual is such a recipient, or because of any requirement of such public assistance, rental assistance, or housing subsidy program.

title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
requirement: Makes it an antitrust violation for rental property owners to pay for or use a coordinator's services, for anyone to perform a coordinating function (algorithmic setting or recommending of rents, lease terms or occupancy using shared competitively sensitive information), or to engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination. Government affordability controls, public free rent estimates, research use and equal-terms brokerage databases are excluded.
penalty: Violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act, P.L.1970, c.73; enforcement under sections 6 through 17 of that act remains applicable.
status_basis: Takes effect on the first day of the twelfth month next following the date of enactment (approved July 20, 2026).

requires.name: residential_dwelling_unit
requires.text: Applies to rental residential dwelling units intended as a primary residence in the State; excludes inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, or detention or correctional facilities.

coverage.summary: Applies to rental property owners, coordinators and other persons dealing with rental residential dwelling units in New Jersey.
coverage.exemptions_summary: Excludes government entities setting rents via affordability controls and certain research, public estimate and brokerage database uses.

precedence.text: A municipality shall be prohibited from enacting an ordinance that conflicts with this act.

quoted_span:
It
shall be unlawful and a violation of the “New Jersey Antitrust Act,” P.L.1970,
c.73 (C.56:9-1 et seq.) for:
a.     a rental property owner, or any agent,
representative, or subcontractor thereof, to receive, subscribe to, contract
for, or otherwise exchange any form of consideration in return for the use of,
the services of a coordinator;

also_supported_by.quoted_span: The FAIR Act prohibits residential rental property owners from using algorithmic revenue management software that collects or processes competitors' nonpublic leasing information to set or recommend rental prices. It also prohibits software providers and other "coordinators" from using such software to facilitate agreements or coordinate pricing among competing residential landlords.

title: New Jersey Security Deposit Law
requirement: Landlords may collect a security deposit of no more than one and one-half times one month's rent, and annual increases may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Deposits must be held in trust in an interest-bearing account, interest belongs to the tenant, and the tenant must receive written notice of the bank and account details within 30 days.
key_value: 1.5 times one month's rent; annual increase up to 10%
penalty: If the tenant does not receive proper notice or interest, the tenant may apply the deposit plus 7% per annum interest to rent.

exempt_if.name: owner_occupied_two_or_three_family
exempt_if.text: The exception is an owner-occupied two-, or three-family dwelling.

exempt_if.name: seasonal_rental
exempt_if.text: This section of the Security Deposit Law does not apply to security deposits for seasonal use or rental (interest-bearing account provisions).

coverage.summary: Applies to most residential rental properties, including mobile homes.
coverage.exemptions_summary: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings are exempt unless the tenant requests coverage in writing, and the interest-account provisions do not apply to seasonal rentals.

quoted_span:
The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than 
one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ). It can be less. Any additional 
yearly security deposit increase may not exceed 10% of the current security deposit.

also_supported_by.quoted_span:
Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security 
deposit, plus interest earned less deductions, to the tenant ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1).

title: Anti-Eviction Act
requirement: A landlord may recover possession of a residential unit only by consent or through court eviction, and must have good cause to evict or fail to renew a lease. Each cause except nonpayment must be described in a written Notice to Quit (and sometimes a Notice to Cease), and a Judgment for Possession must be entered before the tenant must move.
key_value: Warrant for possession not issuable until 3 business days after judgment; tenant then has 3 business days to move

requires.name: residential_rental
requires.text: applies to most residential rental properties including single-family homes, mobile homes and land in a mobile home park, apartment buildings, and complexes, and rooming and boarding homes

exempt_if.name: owner_occupied_small
exempt_if.text: two- or three-unit owner-occupied premises with two (2) or fewer rental units

exempt_if.name: transient_guest
exempt_if.text: hotel guests, motel guests, or guest houses rented to a transient guest or seasonal tenant

exempt_if.name: family_trust_unit
exempt_if.text: a unit held in trust on behalf of a member of the immediate family who is developmentally disabled and permanently occupies the unit

coverage.summary: Applies to most residential rentals including houses, mobile homes, apartments and rooming/boarding homes.
coverage.exemptions_summary: Does not apply to certain small owner-occupied premises, transient or seasonal hotel/motel guests, and units held in trust for a developmentally disabled family member.

quoted_span:
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a 
lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.

also_supported_by.quoted_span:
No landlord of residential rental properties except t hose in owner occupied two or three 
family dwellings, motels or hotels, transient, or seasonal units may fail to renew any lease, 
regardless of whether it is written or oral unless they have good cause not to renew the lease.
Listed below are the statutory grounds for eviction as set forth in the Anti-Eviction Statute.

Tenants of landlord-occupied two- and three-family dwellings can be removed only when 
a court issues an order for eviction.

title: P.L. 2025, c.405 (Residential rental property application fee limit)
requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property that exceeds $50. The cap is adjusted each January 1 by the percent change in the regional CPI, only when that change is above zero.
key_value: $50 cap, adjusted annually for CPI
penalty: Up to $500 for a first offense, up to $750 for a second, and up to $1,000 for each subsequent offense. The amount wrongfully charged is taken from the penalty and remitted to the applicant.
status_basis: Takes effect on the first day of the fourth month next following the date of enactment (approved January 20, 2026).

exempt_if.text: a dwelling unit located in a one-family or two-family dwelling that is offered for rent

exempt_if.name: real_estate_licensee_not_landlord
exempt_if.text: a licensee of the New Jersey Real Estate Commission, unless the licensee is the landlord of the residential rental property

coverage.summary: Applies to application fees for residential rental property leased or subleased for dwelling purposes.
coverage.exemptions_summary: Does not apply to units in one- or two-family dwellings or to NJ Real Estate Commission licensees who are not the landlord.

quoted_span:
A landlord, or
agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply
to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which
exceeds $50.

title: Rent Control Ordinance, Chapter 260 of the Jersey City Municipal Code
requirement: Jersey City administers and enforces a rent control ordinance regulating rent increases, with landlord applications for capital improvement, vacancy and hardship increases and tenant petitions for illegal rent or failure to maintain services. All 1-4 unit properties are exempt from rent control.
citation: Chapter 260 of the Jersey City Municipal Code

exempt_if.text: All 1-4 Unit Properties are exempt from rent control

coverage.exemptions_summary: Properties with 1-4 units are exempt, and the ordinance allows other permitted exemptions by owner request.

quoted_span:
The Office of Landlord Tenant Relations administers and enforces the
Rent Control Ordinance, Chapter 260
of the Jersey City Municipal Code and provides education, information and referrals to city residents in connection with landlord/tenant issues.

title: Rent Control/Rent Increases in New Jersey (Anti-Eviction Act notice and unconscionability standard; Newly Constructed Multiple Dwellings Law)
requirement: The State sets no rent control. Municipalities may adopt rent control ordinances, and a landlord may raise rent only by terminating the lease and giving proper written notice. The increase must not be unconscionable and must comply with local ordinances. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years, and rents may not be raised to cover costs of a condominium or cooperative conversion.
key_value: No state cap; newly constructed multiple dwellings exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion

coverage.summary: State notice and unconscionability rules apply to residential rent increases, with any rent caps set by municipal ordinance.
coverage.exemptions_summary: Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction, and government-subsidized rents may also be exempt.

precedence.text: Municipalities may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

quoted_span:
The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

also_supported_by.quoted_span:
If a building is converted to a condominium or cooperative form of ownership, or to fee 
simple ownership of units, rents may not be increased to cover cos ts resulting solely from the 
conversion (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.31).

title: Fair Chance in Housing Act
requirement: Housing providers may not ask about or consider an applicant's criminal record until after a conditional offer. They may never consider non-conviction, expunged, sealed, pardoned, vacated or juvenile records. After an offer, they may consider only listed serious convictions within set look-back periods, and a withdrawal needs an individualized assessment and written notice.
key_value: Post-offer look-back: 6 years for first-degree, 4 years for second/third-degree, 1 year for fourth-degree indictable offenses
penalty: Civil penalty up to $1,000 for a first violation, $5,000 for a second within five years, and $10,000 for two or more others within seven years; the director may also order the application fee returned and up to $1,000 paid to the applicant.
status_basis: Takes effect on the first day of the seventh month next following the date of enactment (approved June 18, 2021).

of not more than four dwelling units

coverage.exemptions_summary: Dwelling units in owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units are excluded.

A housing
provider
shall not make any oral or written inquiry
regarding an applicant’s criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.

title: New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (LAD) – source of lawful income protection
requirement: Landlords may not discriminate in housing based on the source of lawful income or the source of lawful rent or mortgage payment, so they cannot deny a Section 8 voucher holder an apartment solely because of that income source.
penalty: Complaints may be filed free with the Division on Civil Rights within 180 days, or in NJ Superior Court within two years of the alleged violation.

exempt_if.name: owner_occupied_two_family
exempt_if.text: The rental of a single apartment or flat in a two-family dwelling, the other occupancy unit of which is occupied by the owner as his/her residence at the time of such rentals

exempt_if.name: owner_occupied_one_family_room_rental
exempt_if.text: The rental of a room or rooms to another person or persons by the owner or occupant of a one-family dwelling occupied by him/her as his/her residence at the time of such rental

coverage.summary: Applies to the sale or rental of all property, including open land, for business or residential purposes.
coverage.exemptions_summary: Exempts rental of one unit in an owner-occupied two-family dwelling and rental of rooms in an owner-occupied one-family dwelling, among other LAD exceptions.

quoted_span:
The LAD also prohibits housing discrimination  based
on the source of lawful income or source of lawful rent
or mortgage payment a tenant or purchaser uses. This
means, for example, that a landlord cannot deny the
lawful recipient of a Section 8 HUD voucher the right to
rent an apartment based solely on that source of lawful
income.
